item.title: How to cook and store oyster mushrooms (pink, blue and pearl)
item.description: Dry sear oyster mushrooms in a hot pan, always cook them, and eat pink within 3 days. Storage days by species and three simple Thanksgiving dishes, cited.
item.content:encoded:
Cook oyster mushrooms in a hot, dry pan first, then add the fat. Raw oysters are about 89% water by USDA data, and they cannot brown until that water cooks off, so a crowded or cool pan steams them grey and rubbery. Tear them into pieces, sear in one layer until the water is gone and the edges brown, then add oil or butter, salt and garlic. Always cook them through. Illinois Extension does not recommend eating specialty mushrooms raw and says 145 °F (63 °C) inside is enough. For storage, use a paper bag in the fridge, never a sealed container. Pearl and blue oyster keep about 5 to 7 days, pink oyster under 3 days, and Ohio State says all oysters are best within 3 days. At room temperature they last only 1 to 3 days.

How do you cook oyster mushrooms?

Hot pan, one layer, no oil at first, and leave them alone. That is the whole trick. Oyster mushrooms are thin and full of water. USDA FoodData Central lists raw oyster mushrooms at 89.2 g of water per 100 g (USDA). Until most of that water is gone, the pan cannot brown them. If the pan is cool or crowded, the water pools and the mushrooms boil in it. That is where the grey, slippery oysters people complain about come from.

So cook in two phases. First drive the water out with high heat in a dry pan. Then add fat and flavor once they start to brown. Utah State Extension gives the same rule for sautéed mushrooms: cook until the liquid is gone or until golden brown (Utah State).

High heat is also a good choice for nutrition. A study that cooked oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus ostreatus) and king oysters four ways found grilling and microwaving kept the nutritional profile best, while boiling and deep frying lost more protein and antioxidant activity. The authors point to browning products from the Maillard reaction as part of why grilled mushrooms scored higher (Roncero-Ramos et al. 2017). A hot dry sear is close to grilling.

How to dry sear oyster mushrooms

  1. Trim off any substrate at the base, then tear the cluster into bite size pieces along the gills. Do not soak them. Brush off debris, or rinse briefly and pat dry, right before cooking.
  2. Heat a heavy skillet, cast iron if you have it, over high heat until it is hot. No oil yet.
  3. Add the mushrooms in a single layer with room between pieces. Cook in batches if they do not fit.
  4. Press them flat with a spatula or a second pan and leave them. They will squeak, give off water, then go quiet as it boils away.
  5. When the edges brown, flip them and brown the other side.
  6. Now add a spoon of oil or butter, a pinch of salt and some garlic or thyme. Toss for about a minute until fragrant.
  7. Make sure they are hot all the way through, then serve right away. Seared oysters go soft as they sit.

Can you eat oyster mushrooms raw?

No. Cook them. University of Illinois Extension does not recommend eating specialty or gourmet mushrooms raw and says all of them should be thoroughly cooked. It also says that because mushrooms are not a high risk food like meat or eggs, cooking them to an internal temperature of 145 °F (63 °C) should be enough (Illinois Extension). Ohio State's home grower guide ends the same way: fully cook any fresh mushrooms (Ohio State).

Thin torn pieces heat through fast. Thick blue caps and king oyster stems take a little longer, so check those.

Should you wash oyster mushrooms?

Only right before you cook them, and only briefly. Illinois Extension notes that USDA does not recommend washing produce, mushrooms included, until just before use, because produce left wet in storage can let bacteria grow (Illinois Extension). Missouri Extension says to clean mushrooms just before using them with a soft brush or a damp paper towel, or a very quick rinse under cold water and a pat dry (Missouri Extension).

Homegrown oysters from a clean block usually need nothing more than trimming the base. Wet mushrooms also fight you in the pan, so dry them well.

How do pink, blue and pearl oysters cook differently?

They all take the same dry sear. What changes is texture and how fast you need to use them.

  • Pink oyster (profile) is the meatiest and the chewiest. Ohio State describes it as meaty and seafood like, and says that fried it can taste like bacon or ham (Ohio State). Cook it hard until crisp at the edges. It is the one to cook the day you pick it.
  • Blue oyster (profile) gives the biggest caps when grown cool. A USDA SARE funded grower booklet says one blue strain grown at 50 to 65 °F (10 to 18 °C) makes large, thick caps (Crosby 2016). Thick caps hold up to a press in the pan, so they sear like a steak.
  • Pearl oyster (profile) is the classic grocery oyster, Pleurotus ostreatus, and the most all purpose. Its clusters tear into even pieces that brown fast.

Golden oyster and king oyster cook the same way. Golden is the most delicate and Ohio State says sautéed in oil it tastes like roasted cashews. King oyster has the thick stem, so slice it into rounds before searing.

Pick at the right stage and every one of them cooks better. Our pearl oyster profile says to harvest when caps flatten and edges just begin to turn up, and Ohio State says picking before the caps curl reduces toughness. How to fruit an oyster mushroom kit covers harvest timing in detail.

How long do oyster mushrooms last in the fridge?

It depends on the species, and on the container. Here are the numbers by species.

OysterFridge, paper bagSource
Pearl oyster (P. ostreatus)5 to 7 daysUniversity of Kentucky; 5 to 7 days at 4 °C in a storage review
Blue oyster (P. ostreatus var. columbinus)5 to 7 days, same species as pearlUniversity of Kentucky; storage review
Pink oyster (P. djamor)Under 3 daysOhio State
Golden oyster (P. citrinopileatus)Shorter than pearl or blue, delicateOhio State
King oyster (P. eryngii)Up to a weekOhio State
Any oyster at room temperature1 to 3 days at 20 to 25 °CStorage review
Any oyster in a sealed containerRots in 1 to 2 daysSARE booklet

The University of Kentucky puts oyster mushrooms at five to seven days under refrigeration, against 12 to 14 for shiitake, and says to refrigerate them right away in paper bags or vented boxes (University of Kentucky). A review of fresh mushroom storage gives P. ostreatus 5 to 7 days at 4 °C and 1 to 3 days at 20 to 25 °C (Castellanos-Reyes et al. 2021). Ohio State gives pink oyster a shelf life of under 3 days, calls golden exceptionally delicate with a shorter shelf life, and says king oyster can stay fresh for up to a week refrigerated (Ohio State).

Those are outer limits. For best texture, Ohio State says to keep oysters in a paper bag in the fridge, not plastic, and use them within three days, because they wilt, dry out and get tough (Ohio State). Our pink oyster profile says the same thing in fewer words: harvest early, shelf life is short.

What is the best way to store oyster mushrooms?

A paper bag, or a container with holes, in the coldest part of the fridge. Never sealed plastic. The SARE booklet stores oysters at 36 to 38 °F (2 to 3 °C) with a cover to slow drying and some holes for air, says they can keep about 10 days that way, and says that in a sealed container the water cannot escape and they rot within 1 to 2 days (Crosby 2016).

Sealed containers are a safety issue too, not just a quality one. Health Canada says storing fresh mushrooms unrefrigerated in an airtight container may promote the growth of bacteria that cause botulism, and says to refrigerate them in a paper bag (Health Canada).

Other rules worth keeping:

  • Do not store them at room temperature (Missouri Extension).
  • Do not wash before storing. Wash right before cooking.
  • Do not pile them deep. The SARE booklet stacks harvested oysters no more than two high because they are fragile.
  • Throw out any that are bruised or spoiled, as Health Canada advises.

Can you freeze oyster mushrooms?

Yes, but cook them first. Health Canada says mushrooms can be frozen only if they are steamed or sautéed first (Health Canada), and Utah State says fresh mushrooms should never be frozen. Sear them, cool them, and freeze them flat in a bag. Missouri Extension says cooked mushrooms are best used within 1 month for quality (Missouri Extension).

Drying is the long keeper. The University of Kentucky says drying, then storing in sealed containers, adds at least six months of shelf life.

What are three simple oyster mushroom dishes for Thanksgiving?

All three start with the dry sear above. Do the searing close to serving time, since seared oysters lose their crisp edges as they sit.

1. Seared oysters with butter, garlic and thyme

Best with pearl or blue oyster. Dry sear the mushrooms in batches until browned. Put them all back in the pan, add butter, a chopped garlic clove and a few thyme leaves, and toss until the butter foams. Finish with salt, pepper and a squeeze of lemon. Serve as a side, or spoon over mashed potatoes or sliced turkey. Utah State notes a little lemon juice also helps mushrooms keep their color.

2. Crispy pink oyster bits for green beans or salad

Best with pink oyster, the one Ohio State says can taste like bacon or ham when fried. Tear it small, dry sear until the water is gone, then add a little more oil than usual and keep cooking, pressing the pieces flat, until they are crisp and dark at the edges. Salt them, drain on a paper towel, and scatter over green beans, a salad or a squash soup right before serving. If you grow pink for color, our Chef's line bright pink oyster profile is built for that; see the Chef's line for the rest.

3. Oyster mushroom gravy

Any oyster works. Sear a pan of torn oysters until well browned, then add butter and an equal amount of flour and stir for a minute. Whisk in stock or turkey drippings a little at a time until it is as thick as you like, and simmer a few minutes. Searing first matters here. Utah State says to sauté mushrooms before adding them to a stew or braise, because they shrink as they cook. The browning is where the gravy gets its flavor.

For a crowd, roasting is easier than batches in a skillet. Utah State roasts mushrooms with salt, pepper and garlic at 400 °F (204 °C) until golden brown. Spread oysters in one layer on a sheet pan with space between pieces, the same as in the skillet, so they roast instead of steam.

How long do cooked oyster mushrooms keep?

Treat them like any other leftover. USDA says to refrigerate cooked food within 2 hours, keep leftovers 3 to 4 days in the fridge, and reheat them to 165 °F (74 °C). Bring gravy to a rolling boil when you reheat it (USDA FSIS). On a long Thanksgiving table, that 2 hour limit is the one people miss.

FAQ

Why are my oyster mushrooms rubbery?

They steamed instead of seared. The pan was too crowded or not hot enough, so the water they gave off had nowhere to go. Cook in a hot dry pan in a single layer, in batches, and wait until the water is gone before you add fat.

Do you eat the stems of oyster mushrooms?

Yes, on pearl, blue and pink, though the base where the cluster joins can be tough. Trim off any substrate and the hardest part of the base. King oyster is grown for its thick stem.

How do you cook pink oyster mushrooms?

Hot and fast, the day you harvest them. Tear them small, dry sear until the edges are crisp, then add oil and salt. Pink has the chewiest texture of the three, and Ohio State says fried it can taste like bacon or ham. Eat it within 3 days at most.

Do pink oyster mushrooms stay pink when cooked?

Do not count on it. Our pink oyster profile notes the color already fades as the mushrooms mature, so harvest early while it is vivid. Grow pink for the flavor and the texture first.

Can you eat oyster mushrooms raw?

No. Illinois Extension does not recommend eating specialty mushrooms raw. Cook them through, to at least 145 °F (63 °C) inside.

Should you store oyster mushrooms in plastic?

No. Use a paper bag or a vented container in the fridge. In a sealed container they hold their own water and can rot within 1 to 2 days.

Which oyster mushroom should I grow for cooking?

Grow the one that fits your room. Blue for a cool room, pink for a warm one, pearl for anything in between. Blue vs pink vs golden oyster compares them side by side, and the grow timeline calculator gives you a harvest date if you are planning one for a holiday.

item.title: Psilocybe cubensis: taxonomy, habitat and what the research documents
item.description: Where P. cubensis sits in fungal taxonomy, where it grows wild, and what genome studies say about its origin and cultivars. Every line cited.
item.content:encoded:
Psilocybe cubensis is a dung-loving mushroom first described from Cuba in 1906 as Stropharia cubensis and moved to Psilocybe by Rolf Singer in 1948. Index Fungorum lists it as the accepted name, with ten synonyms, and both Index Fungorum and NCBI Taxonomy now place it in the family Agrocybaceae. In the wild it lives on the dung of cattle and other large grazers in warm regions of the Americas, Southeast Asia and Australia. A 2026 study found its closest wild relative, the new African species P. ochraceocentrata, split from it about 1.5 million years ago. A 2023 genome study of 124 genomes found the commercial cultivars, including Golden Teacher and Penis Envy, are highly inbred compared with a naturalized wild population in Australia. Psilocybin and psilocin are Schedule I under US federal law and the 1971 UN Convention.

Short answer

Psilocybe cubensis is the best known psilocybin mushroom and one of the most studied. Its name, its family, its wild range and the history of its cultivars have all been revised by DNA work in the last few years, so a lot of what gets repeated online is out of date.

This post is a research summary. Every claim below points to a taxonomy database, a government source or a peer reviewed paper with a DOI. It is not a guide to finding, growing or using any mushroom, and it makes no health claims. Shroom Labs does not sell spores, cultures or psilocybin products.

How is Psilocybe cubensis classified?

The species was first published in 1906 by Franklin Sumner Earle as Stropharia cubensis, in volume 1 of the annual report of Cuba's Estación Central Agronómica, page 240. The type came from Cuba. NCBI Taxonomy lists the holotype as New York Botanical Garden herbarium specimen NY 761563.

Rolf Singer moved it to Psilocybe in 1948, in Sydowia volume 2, page 37. That combination, Psilocybe cubensis (Earle) Singer, is the current name in Index Fungorum.

RankNameSource
KingdomFungiIndex Fungorum 290107
PhylumBasidiomycotaIndex Fungorum 290107
ClassAgaricomycetesIndex Fungorum 290107
OrderAgaricalesIndex Fungorum 290107
FamilyAgrocybaceaeIndex Fungorum 290107 and NCBI Taxonomy 181762
GenusPsilocybeIndex Fungorum 290107
SpeciesPsilocybe cubensis (Earle) Singer 1948Index Fungorum 290107

Older books put the species in Strophariaceae, which is where Index Fungorum still files the original name Stropharia cubensis. If you read an older paper that says Strophariaceae, it is the same mushroom.

Synonyms

Kew's species record, which takes its names from Index Fungorum, lists ten synonyms. The ones you are most likely to see in older literature:

  • Stropharia cubensis Earle, the original 1906 name
  • Stropharia cyanescens Murrill
  • Naematoloma caerulescens Pat.
  • Hypholoma caerulescens (Pat.) Sacc. and Trotter
  • Psilocybe cubensis var. caerulescens (Pat.) Singer and A.H. Sm.
  • Psilocybe cubensis var. cyanescens (Murrill) Singer and A.H. Sm.
  • Psilocybe fasciata Hongo

Where it sits in the genus

A 2024 PNAS study by Bradshaw and colleagues sequenced 71 fungarium specimens, 23 of them type specimens, and built a tree from 2,983 single copy gene families. They put the genus at about 165 species, with the stem lineage arising about 67 million years ago. They also found the psilocybin genes come in two different orders that match a deep split in the genus. The original order was first reported from P. cubensis and P. serbica.

Where does Psilocybe cubensis grow wild?

On dung. Both major recent papers describe it as a dung specialist tied to livestock, mostly cattle. McTaggart and colleagues (2023) call livestock dung its niche. Bradshaw and colleagues (2026) describe it as a widespread dung specialist and say its specialization on domesticated cattle dung likely traces back to an ancestor that lived on the dung of large wild herbivores.

The 2026 study's climate models place its likely historical range across the Americas, Southeast Asia and Australasia. The authors say they know of no authenticated record of P. cubensis from Africa. African collections once filed under that name turned out to be a different species (see below).

Australia is the best studied population. McTaggart and colleagues sequenced 38 Australian isolates and found a population that went through a sharp bottleneck when it was introduced, then recovered and kept relatively high genetic diversity. They describe it as naturalized, spread with cattle, and note it has caused accidental poisonings there since the 1940s.

Where did Psilocybe cubensis come from?

The common story is that it reached the Americas with cattle brought from Africa and Europe around 1500 CE. The 2026 Proceedings B paper by Bradshaw and colleagues tested that by sequencing type specimens of every known and accessible African Psilocybe species.

What they found:

  • African specimens that had been called P. cubensis are a separate species, which they named Psilocybe ochraceocentrata. It is the closest known wild relative of P. cubensis.
  • The two species last shared a common ancestor about 1.5 million years ago, with a 95% range of about 710,000 to 2.55 million years. That is long before cattle were domesticated.
  • Both species live on the dung of large herbivores.

So the cattle story may explain how P. cubensis moved around in the last 500 years, but it does not explain where the lineage started. The authors frame their range maps as hypotheses to test, not settled history.

What does the research document about its chemistry?

Psilocybin was first isolated and named in 1958 by Albert Hofmann and colleagues, from a different species, Psilocybe mexicana. Two later papers worked out how P. cubensis makes it and why it turns blue.

  • Biosynthesis. Fricke, Blei and Hoffmeister (2017) characterized four enzymes, PsiD, PsiK, PsiM and PsiH, and made psilocybin enzymatically from 4-hydroxy-L-tryptophan using three of them.
  • The blue bruise. Lenz and colleagues (published online in 2019) found two P. cubensis enzymes behind the blue color on damaged tissue. PsiP removes the phosphate from psilocybin to give psilocin, and PsiL oxidizes psilocin. The oxidized units link into chains of roughly 3 to 13 units, and those are the blue products.
  • Genome. McKernan and colleagues (2021) published a draft reference genome of 46.6 million base pairs, 46% GC, in 32 contigs. The psilocybin gene cluster sits on a single 3.2 million base pair contig.

I am leaving out potency numbers on purpose. They vary between samples, they are not what this post is about, and Shroom Labs does not publish dosing information.

What do Golden Teacher, B+ and Penis Envy mean genetically?

They are cultivar names used in trade, not species. All three of our profiles list the species as Psilocybe cubensis.

The best data on what those names mean comes from McTaggart and colleagues (2023), who compared the 38 Australian genomes with 86 genomes of commercial cultivars, 124 in total. Their results:

  • The cultivars sorted into five groups: Blue Magnolia (20 genomes), Golden Teacher (37), Luminous (15), Malabar (8) and P-envy (6). B+ is not one of the named groups.
  • Cultivars show the marks of selfing and clonal propagation: low genetic diversity, low heterozygosity and few mating type alleles.
  • Golden Teacher and P-envy were the least heterozygous groups. Golden Teacher had a mean inbreeding coefficient of 0.784 and P-envy 0.811, where 1 means completely inbred.
  • The Australian population carried 13 HD and 9 PR mating type alleles. Golden Teacher carried 3 and 5, and P-envy 2 and 5.
  • Most cultivars were founded from related populations, and the psilocybin gene alleles are identical across most of them.

In plain terms, a lot of differently named cultivars are close relatives. For the profiles on this site, read the cultivar name as a label, not a pedigree. The Golden Teacher, B+ and Penis Envy pages list published environmental conditions for reference and research only. They are not cultivation instructions. For a different Psilocybe species, see the P. cyanescens profile.

Legal status, checked 2026-11-23

Every row was checked on 2026-11-23. This is a summary, not legal advice. For US state detail on spores and psilocybin, see are mushroom spores legal.

United States (federal)Psilocybin (code 7437) and psilocyn (code 7438) are Schedule I, 21 CFR 1308.11(d)(29) and (30)eCFR 21 CFR 1308.11
OregonMeasure 109 (November 2020) directs the Oregon Health Authority to license and regulate psilocybin products and services. Federal Schedule I still appliesOregon Health Authority

FAQ

What family is Psilocybe cubensis in?

Index Fungorum and NCBI Taxonomy both place it in Agrocybaceae, order Agaricales, as of 2026-11-23. Older sources say Strophariaceae, which is where the original 1906 name Stropharia cubensis was filed.

Who named Psilocybe cubensis?

Franklin Sumner Earle described it from Cuba in 1906 as Stropharia cubensis. Rolf Singer transferred it to Psilocybe in 1948, which is why the full name is Psilocybe cubensis (Earle) Singer.

Where is Psilocybe cubensis native?

That is still open. It grows on cattle and other large herbivore dung in warm parts of the Americas, Southeast Asia and Australasia. A 2026 study found its closest wild relative in sub-Saharan Africa and dated their split to about 1.5 million years ago, and the same study reports no authenticated African records of P. cubensis itself.

Are Golden Teacher and Penis Envy different species?

No. Both are cultivars of P. cubensis. A 2023 genome study found them among the least genetically diverse cultivar groups, with signs of long term inbreeding and clonal propagation.

Why does Psilocybe cubensis bruise blue?

Damaged tissue starts an enzyme cascade. PsiP turns psilocybin into psilocin and PsiL oxidizes psilocin, which then links into blue chains, according to Lenz and colleagues (2019).

Is Psilocybe cubensis legal?

Psilocybin and psilocin are Schedule I under US federal law and the 1971 UN Convention. A few places run regulated programs, listed in the table above with sources. Check the current law where you live.

item.title: Is that green mold on my mushroom substrate, or healthy mycelium?
item.description: How to tell Trichoderma green mold from healthy white, brown or blue-tinged mycelium in a photo, what to do with the block, and how to stop it next time.
item.content:encoded:
Healthy mycelium is white and stays white, or turns an even brown on a shiitake block or blue-gray on cool blue oyster pins. Green or blue-green powder is mold. The catch is that Trichoderma, the usual green mold, starts as a dense white patch that looks just like mycelium, then turns green as it makes spores. Its best growth is at 27 to 30 °C (81 to 86 °F), and one isolate grew 30 to 40 times faster than oyster mycelium in a lab test. In a survey of green contamination in shiitake houses, 63% of isolates were Trichoderma and 9% were Penicillium. So photograph any odd white patch every 24 hours. If it goes green, bag the block and remove it. Only a small blue-green spot on a sealed, still colonizing bag is worth isolating and watching.

How do you tell green mold from healthy mycelium in a photo?

Look at color first, then texture, then how it changes over a day or two. Our contamination guide covers every kind of contamination. This post zooms in on the green and blue-green ones, because they cause the most confusion and they are the ones that hide inside white growth at the start.

What you see in the photoMost likelyWhat to do
Even white, cottony or ropey growth across the blockHealthy myceliumNothing. Keep going.
A denser, brighter white patch that looks different from the restCould be early Trichoderma, could be healthyPhotograph it every 24 h
White patch with a green center or green edgesTrichoderma making sporesBag and remove the block
Dark forest green, powdery, spreadingTrichodermaBag and remove the block
Small blue-green spotsOften Penicillium, can be other moldsRemove if opened, isolate if sealed
A brown line where white growth meets a patchMushroom mycelium reacting to a moldTreat it as contaminated
Brown, even, leathery skin on a shiitake blockNormal shiitake browningNothing. This is what you want.
Blue-gray pins or caps on a blue oysterNormal pigmentNothing
Yellow or amber drops on white myceliumNormal liquid from the myceliumNothing

Two lab facts explain why this table needs a time column. Penn State Extension describes green mold as dense white growth that is followed by heavy green sporulation. A 2024 study of an oyster farm said the same thing: at first the mold could not be told apart from the oyster mycelium, because both were dense and white, and the green came later (Ajis, Tan and Chai 2024). One photo cannot tell them apart. Two photos a day apart often can.

What does Trichoderma look like at each stage?

Trichoderma is a genus, not one mold. On oyster mushrooms the usual culprits are Trichoderma pleurotum and T. pleuroticola, which were confirmed on oyster farms in Europe, Iran and South Korea, and T. pleuroticola also lives in soil and wood in the United States and Canada (Komoń-Zelazowska et al. 2007). On shiitake, a two year survey of contaminated substrate in China turned up 14 different Trichoderma species from 150 samples (Cao et al. 2024).

What they share is a pattern you can see:

  1. White and dense. A patch that is thicker or fluffier than the mycelium around it.
  2. Green edges or a green center. Penn State's IPM guide for mushroom farms says the patch starts out gray, turns white along the edges and goes green as it sporulates.
  3. Dark green powder. The patch spreads and the spores dust off if the block is bumped.

Not every Trichoderma is green on day one. In a Korean extension study, T. harzianum colonies turned bright green, T. cf. virens was yellowish green, and T. longibrachiatum was yellow on lab agar (Choi et al. 2003). That is one more reason to judge by change over time, not a single color.

What is the brown line between the mold and the white mycelium?

That line is the mushroom fighting back, and it is a warning sign. Penn State notes browning of button mushroom mycelium and small pins breaking down at the advancing edge of green mold. In lab plates of shiitake against Trichoderma, the shiitake put out more brown substances and formed brown lines where the two met (Cao et al. 2024). The 2026 oyster lab work showed the same kind of discoloration where Trichoderma overgrew the mushroom (Shan et al. 2026).

So a white block with a sharp brown border around one patch is not bruising. Treat it as contaminated, even if the green has not shown yet.

Is brown or blue on my block ever normal?

Yes, and these are the three that fool people most:

  • Shiitake turns brown on purpose. Our shiitake profile runs 42 days of colonization and then 21 days of browning at 21 °C, because the block forms a protective brown skin before it fruits. In a Japanese sawdust study, healthy shiitake bags were fully white by day 26 and covered in brown pigmented mycelium after day 61 (Terashima, Igusa and Ohga 2002). Even, leathery brown is good. Fuzzy green on top of the brown is not.
  • Blue oyster really is blue. Our blue oyster profile colonizes at 22 °C and pins at 15 °C, and notes that the deep color holds better below 18 °C. Blue-gray pins with a cap and stem shape are the crop. Blue-green powder on flat substrate is mold.
  • Yellow drops are fine. Amber liquid on white mycelium is normal and is covered in the contamination guide.

The test for all three is shape. Mushrooms and healthy mycelium have structure: strands, ropes, pins, caps. Mold on the surface is a flat, powdery mat with no structure.

Is blue-green mold the same as green mold?

Not always. When Thai researchers collected green spore molds from shiitake logs and sawdust bags in five production houses, they got 43 isolates: 62.8% Trichoderma, 20.9% Gliocladium, 9.3% Penicillium and 7.0% Aspergillus (Pukahuta et al. 2000). Many blue-green spots are Penicillium, but you cannot confirm the genus from a phone photo.

The difference matters, at least on shiitake. In that Japanese study, bags infected with Penicillium brevicompactum at the same time as spawning showed spores by day 6, but by day 26 the shiitake had grown over them, and yield and mushroom size were no different from clean bags, though some of those bags gave more misshapen mushrooms. Bags infected with T. harzianum on any of the four test days were covered in spores and fatally damaged (Terashima, Igusa and Ohga 2002). The University of Florida grow guide lists blue, green, black and yellow spots all as signs of contamination, and calls out Trichoderma for its rapid greenish growth (Liao et al., UF/IFAS SS662).

What should you do with a block that has green mold?

Bag it and get it out. The steps for safe removal and cleanup are in the contamination guide, and we will not repeat them here. Three points that are specific to green mold:

  • Do not scrape it off. The white stage you cannot see is often bigger than the green you can. Penn State calls out people and equipment as the main way green mold moves around a farm. A spoon that touched the patch is now carrying it.
  • Do not save the fruit for dinner. The UF guide says partially contaminated bags may still give one flush. That is a farm yield note, not a food safety pass. On a home kit, mushrooms from a moldy block are not worth the risk.
  • Look at the block's neighbors. A 2024 study found water was the main source of green mold on the oyster farm it studied, followed by air in the growing house (Ajis, Tan and Chai 2024). If you mist several blocks from one bottle, check every block that bottle touched.

Can you save a block with a small blue-green spot?

Sometimes, if the bag is still sealed. Here is the one case where we wait instead of tossing:

  • The bag has never been opened and is still colonizing.
  • The spot is small, blue-green, and not a dense white patch going green.
  • There is no brown border around it.

Move that bag away from your other grows, leave it sealed, and photograph it every 24 hours. If white mycelium grows over the spot, as the Penicillium did on shiitake in the Japanese study, carry on. If the spot grows, turns dark green, or gets a brown border, it is done. Once a bag is open or fruiting, skip the wait and remove it.

Why does green mold show up in the first place?

Heat is the big one. In a Korean extension study, Trichoderma isolates from oyster farms grew best at 27 to 30 °C, and T. longibrachiatum could still grow at 37 °C while growing 30 to 40 times faster than the oyster mycelium (Choi et al. 2003). A University of Szeged dissertation on mushroom Trichoderma summarizes work showing a substrate bag can heat itself to 30 °C during spawn run from the mycelium's own metabolism, that Trichoderma growth peaked at 30 °C and stopped at 15 °C, and that Trichoderma grew three times faster than oyster mycelium at 25 °C (Hatvani 2008).

Compare that with the colonization temperatures in our own profiles:

ProfileColonization temperatureDays
Blue oyster22 °C12
Lion's mane22 °C16
Pearl oyster24 °C14
Shiitake24 °C42
Golden oyster25 °C12
Pink oyster27 °C10

Most of them sit a few degrees under the Trichoderma sweet spot. A block in a warm cupboard, or one sitting on top of a fridge, can easily drift into it. Pink oyster colonizes right at the bottom of that range, which is one reason a fast, clean spawn run matters so much for it. Shiitake spends six weeks colonizing, so a small mistake has a long time to grow.

The other cause surprises people: clean substrate can be easier for Trichoderma to take over. An Argentine study sprayed Trichoderma spores onto straw, grain and sawdust after different treatments and then spawned them with oyster mushroom. Trichoderma could not grow on substrate that was not sterilized, sterilized substrate favored it, and growing alongside the mushroom helped it. Hot water at 60 °C for 30 minutes or 36 hours in alkaline lime water cut contamination best (Colavolpe, Jaramillo Mejía and Albertó 2014). Sterile substrate has no other microbes to defend it, so one spore that lands at spawning has the place to itself.

How do you stop green mold next time?

  • Keep colonization at the low end of the profile. Use the profile temperature, not "warm." If the room runs warm, check that the block is not heating itself above that.
  • Spawn fast and clean. The UF guide says to inoculate pasteurized straw as soon as it has drained and cooled, and to clean the work surface and room first. It pasteurizes straw at 165 °F (74 °C) for 1 to 2 hours and spawns at 5 to 10%.
  • Leave sterile bags sealed until they are white all the way through. Sterile substrate has no backup defense, so every opening before full colonization is a risk.
  • Do not share tools or water between a suspect block and clean ones. Penn State and the 2024 farm study both point at people, equipment and water as the way green mold moves.
  • Drop the temperature for fruiting. The Hatvani dissertation summarizes advice to keep the room at 15 to 18 °C after spawn run to slow green mold. Our pearl and king oyster profiles already fruit in that range, and blue oyster a little below it.
  • Retire spent blocks. A block that has given its flushes has little defense left. The contamination guide covers late mold on spent blocks.

How to check a suspicious patch with photos

  1. Take a photo in daylight or under the same white light, with the whole block and the patch in frame.
  2. Take a close-up of the patch from about 10 cm (4 in), and put a coin or ruler next to the bag so you can judge size later.
  3. Do not open the bag, press it, or wipe the patch.
  4. Take the same two photos from the same angle 24 hours later, and again at 48 hours.
  5. Compare them side by side. Spreading green, a new green center, or a brown border means Trichoderma is likely. Bag and remove the block.
  6. If it stays white and blends into the rest, it was mycelium. If you still are not sure, post the photo set on the grow feed for a second opinion.

Most of the time the answer is in the 24 hour photo. If your kit is doing nothing at all rather than growing something odd, start with mushroom grow kit not growing instead.

FAQ

Is green mold on a mushroom block Trichoderma?

Usually. In a survey of green spore molds from shiitake houses, 62.8% of isolates were Trichoderma. The rest were Gliocladium, Penicillium and Aspergillus. You cannot confirm the genus at home, but the handling is the same: bag and remove the block.

Does Trichoderma start out white?

Yes. Penn State describes green mold as dense white growth followed by green sporulation, and a 2024 oyster farm study said the early mold could not be told apart from oyster mycelium. Photograph any unusual white patch every 24 hours.

What temperature does green mold like?

Trichoderma isolates from oyster farms grew best at 27 to 30 °C (81 to 86 °F) in a Korean study. Work summarized in a University of Szeged dissertation found it stopped growing at 15 °C. Keeping colonization near 22 to 24 °C and fruiting cooler helps.

Can mushrooms beat green mold on their own?

Rarely. In a Japanese shiitake study, bags infected with Trichoderma harzianum were fatally damaged no matter when the infection happened. Penicillium was overgrown by the shiitake. Do not count on a block winning against green mold.

Is blue-green mold Penicillium?

Often, but you cannot confirm it from a photo. In the shiitake house survey, Penicillium was 9.3% of green spore isolates and Trichoderma was 62.8%, so treat any blue-green spot on an opened block as contamination.

Why is my shiitake block turning brown?

That is normal. Shiitake forms a protective brown skin before fruiting. Our shiitake profile gives it 21 days of browning at 21 °C after colonization. Even brown is good. Green fuzz on top of it is mold.

  • Penn State Extension, Basic IPM Practices for Organic Mushroom Farms: Fungal Diseases of Mushrooms, for gray then white edges then green, dark green spores, and avoiding people, equipment and plastic as vectors
  • Ajis, Tan and Chai 2024, Green mould contamination of Pleurotus pulmonarius cultivation in Malaysia, Fungal Biology 128(7), for early mold looking like oyster mycelium, and water then air as sources
  • Komoń-Zelazowska et al. 2007, Trichoderma species cause green mold disease in oyster mushroom farms worldwide, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 73, for T. pleurotum and T. pleuroticola and where they were found
  • Cao et al. 2024, Diversity of Trichoderma species associated with green mold contaminating substrates of Lentinula edodes, Frontiers in Microbiology 14:1288585, for 14 species from 150 samples and brown antagonistic lines
  • Choi et al. 2003, Physiological characteristics of green mold (Trichoderma spp.) isolated from oyster mushroom, Mycobiology 31(3), for 27 to 30 °C optimum, growth at 37 °C, 30 to 40 times faster than Pleurotus, and colony colors

item.title: Blue vs pink vs golden oyster mushrooms: which should you grow?
item.description: Blue oyster fits a cool room, pink a warm one, golden sits in between. Temperatures, days to harvest, shelf life and flavor side by side, cited.
item.content:encoded:
Pick the oyster that matches your room. Grow blue oyster if the room runs cool, pink oyster if it runs warm, and golden oyster if it sits around 21 °C (70 °F) and you will keep it indoors. Our profiles fruit blue at 14 °C (57 °F), golden at 21 °C (70 °F) and pink at 24 °C (75 °F). Pink is the fastest at 20 days from spawn to the end of the first harvest, then golden at 24 and blue at 25. Blue keeps the longest, about 5 to 7 days in the fridge, while Ohio State puts pink under 3 days and calls golden delicate with a shorter shelf life. For a first grow, blue is the safest pick. Golden oyster is invasive in North American forests, so never grow it outdoors or compost the spent block.

Which oyster mushroom should you grow: blue, pink or golden?

The one that likes the temperature your room already has. All three are oyster mushrooms in the genus Pleurotus, all three fruit from the same kind of hardwood or straw block, and all three want damp air, plenty of fresh air and some light. The big difference is heat. Blue oyster wants it cool, pink oyster wants it warm, and golden oyster sits between them.

That matters more than any other choice you make. A small chamber or a tote on a counter mostly follows the room. Our own chamber profiles say it plainly: there is no heater or cooler, so a temperature target only holds if the room sits near it. Fighting your room for three weeks is how a first grow goes wrong.

  • Cool room, about 10 to 18 °C (50 to 64 °F): blue oyster.
  • Normal to warm room, about 18 to 24 °C (64 to 75 °F): golden oyster, kept indoors.
  • Warm room or summer with no air conditioning, 24 °C (75 °F) and up: pink oyster.
  • First grow ever: blue oyster, unless your room is warm. Then pink.

How do blue, pink and golden oyster compare side by side?

The growing numbers below are from our free blue oyster, pink oyster and golden oyster profiles. The published ranges, shelf life, and flavor rows are from the sources listed at the end.

Blue oysterPink oysterGolden oyster
SpeciesPleurotus ostreatus var. columbinusPleurotus djamorPleurotus citrinopileatus
Colonization12 days at 22 °C (72 °F)10 days at 27 °C (81 °F)12 days at 25 °C (77 °F)
Pinning4 days at 15 °C (59 °F), 94%3 days at 24 °C (75 °F), 92%4 days at 22 °C (72 °F), 93%
Fruiting9 days at 14 °C (57 °F), 87%7 days at 24 °C (75 °F), 86%8 days at 21 °C (70 °F), 87%
Fruiting warning band in the profile10 to 20 °C (50 to 68 °F)18 to 32 °C (64 to 90 °F)16 to 26 °C (61 to 79 °F)
Published fruiting range12 to 18 °C (54 to 64 °F) on spawn grow cards; 10 to 18 °C (50 to 65 °F) for a cool blue strain20 to 30 °C (68 to 86 °F); 24 to 32 °C (75 to 90 °F) at Ohio State18 to 30 °C (64 to 86 °F); 24 to 32 °C (75 to 90 °F) at Ohio State
Spawn to end of first harvest25 days20 days24 days
From a fully colonized kit13 days10 days12 days
Shelf lifeAbout 5 to 7 days refrigerated, the oyster normUnder 3 daysShort; Ohio State calls it delicate
Flavor and textureLarge caps, thick when grown coolMeaty, seafood like, chewy; fried, it can taste like bacon or hamFragrant and delicate; sautéed in oil it tastes like roasted cashews
Tagged beginner in our libraryYesYesNo
Cold limitCold blue strains fruit down to 2 °C (35 °F)A pink strain did not survive below 4 °C (40 °F)Profile warns below 16 °C (61 °F)

All three profiles use the same light: dark while colonizing, then 12 hours a day at about 92 lux with a blue heavy mix. The fan schedule is the same too, about 40 seconds every 10 minutes while fruiting. So the only setting you really choose by species is temperature. Do mushrooms need light? explains the light numbers.

Note the published ranges run warmer than our profiles for pink and golden. Ohio State lists both at 24 to 32 °C (75 to 90 °F) for fruiting. Our profiles sit at the cool end of each range on purpose, where the color holds and the stems stay short, and the warning bands show how far the room can drift before it matters.

Which oyster grows best in a cold room?

Blue oyster. Its profile pins at 15 °C (59 °F) and fruits at 14 °C (57 °F), and the profile only warns once the room drops below 10 °C (50 °F) or climbs above 20 °C (68 °F). A winter basement, a cool garage, or a spare room with the heat off are all fine.

Cool air is also what keeps it blue. The profile note says the deep color holds better below 18 °C (64 °F), and in a warm chamber blues fade toward grey and the stems stretch. A USDA SARE funded grower booklet says the same about one blue strain: best grown at 50 to 65 °F (10 to 18 °C), with large caps that come in thick and a frosty color when grown cool (Crosby 2016).

Blue oyster is not one fixed thing. Ohio State separates cold blue strains, which fruit at 35 to 50 °F (2 to 10 °C) and need a cold shock, from warm blue strains that fruit at 60 to 85 °F (16 to 29 °C) and fade from blue to steel grey as they mature (Ohio State). Our profile is set for the common middle: a 14 °C (57 °F) fruiting room.

Do not try pink in a cold room. Its profile summary says it stalls and fades in the cold.

Which oyster grows best in a warm room?

Pink oyster. It is a tropical species. Its profile colonizes at 27 °C (81 °F), the warmest of the three, and fruits at 24 °C (75 °F), with no warning until the room passes 32 °C (90 °F). A 2024 study of pink oyster found the mycelium grew best at 24 to 28 °C and the species grew well up to 30 °C (Chowdhury et al. 2024). A summer apartment with no air conditioning suits it.

Golden oyster is the other warm room option and the better fit if the room sits right around 21 °C (70 °F), which is where its profile fruits. Its warning band runs 16 to 26 °C (61 to 79 °F), so it handles a normal heated home.

There is a limit. The same SARE booklet ran a summer grow in a barn where the room swung between 75 and 95 °F (24 and 35 °C) and called that extremely hot for most mushrooms, likely part of why its yellow oyster yields were poor (Crosby 2016). Past about 30 °C (86 °F), even pink is near its edge.

Which oyster is best for a beginner?

Blue oyster, if your room is cool to normal. Ohio State names pearl or blue oyster as the easy starting point, with a wide range of growing conditions from 50 to 80 °F (10 to 27 °C) (Ohio State). Blue keeps longest after harvest, so a picking day that slips by one day is not a loss.

Pink oyster is the beginner pick for a warm room. It is the fastest profile in our library at 20 days, and Ohio State notes it grows on cardboard, paper, coffee grounds and pasteurized straw. Grow oyster mushrooms on coffee grounds covers that route. The catch is timing. Pink has to be picked young and eaten fast.

Golden oyster is the one we do not tag as beginner. It is not hard to fruit, but it is fragile, it needs plenty of fresh air to keep stems short, and it carries the invasive species problem below. If your stems run long on any of these three, leggy mushroom stems walks through the fixes.

How long does each one take to grow?

Pink is fastest, golden and blue are close behind. From the start of colonization to the end of the first harvest, the profiles run 20 days for pink, 24 for golden and 25 for blue. From a kit that arrives fully colonized, cut that to 10, 12 and 13 days. Grower guides land in the same place. The SARE booklet puts the harvest about 5 to 10 days after a block goes into fruiting conditions, and Ohio State says pink fruits in 7 to 10 days.

How long does it take to grow mushrooms? has the same numbers for every species, and the grow timeline calculator turns a start date into calendar dates for each stage. If you are starting from a kit, how to fruit an oyster mushroom kit has the day by day steps.

How long do blue, pink and golden oysters keep after harvest?

Blue keeps longest, pink keeps shortest, and golden is close to pink.

  • Blue oyster. Oyster mushrooms keep 5 to 7 days in the fridge, per the University of Kentucky. A review of fresh mushroom storage gives P. ostreatus, the species blue oyster belongs to, 5 to 7 days at 4 °C and 1 to 3 days at 20 to 25 °C (Castellanos-Reyes et al. 2021). The SARE booklet says oysters stored at 36 to 38 °F (2 to 3 °C) in a container that breathes can keep about 10 days.
  • Pink oyster. Ohio State gives it a shelf life of under 3 days, and the SARE booklet calls its storage and shelf life limited, good for a farmers market but not for wholesale. Our profile says to harvest early and while the color is still vivid, because the pink fades as the fruits mature.
  • Golden oyster. Ohio State calls it exceptionally delicate with a shorter shelf life. Plan to cook it the day you pick it.

For all three, Ohio State's advice is a paper bag in the fridge, not plastic, and use within three days for the best texture. Harvest before the cap edges flatten or flip up. The SARE booklet says a slight roll on the edge keeps the best texture and storability, and limits spore release.

What do blue, pink and golden oysters taste like?

Each one cooks differently, which is a good reason to grow more than one.

  • Pink is the meatiest. Ohio State describes a meaty, seafood like, umami taste and a chewy texture that can taste like bacon or ham when fried.
  • Golden is the most fragrant. Ohio State ranks it among the tastier oysters and says sautéed in oil it tastes like roasted cashews. Michigan's invasive species program calls the flavor nutty.
  • Blue is the classic oyster, and the one that holds up as a big cap. Grown cool, its caps come in large and thick.

Light changes golden oyster too. A 2025 study grew golden oyster under 12 hours of pure blue light and got stems 12.5% shorter than under white light, fuller color, and more of the umami and sweet amino acids. Red and far red light gave pale, soft mushrooms (Chen et al. 2025). Our golden oyster deep yellow profile is built on that result.

Is golden oyster invasive?

Yes, in North America. Golden oyster is native to eastern Asia. A 2025 study by the University of Wisconsin and the USDA Forest Service Center for Forest Mycology Research found it escaped into North American forests around 2010 and has since been reported in 25 US states and one Canadian province. In dead elm trees where it grew, the mix of fungi changed and the number of fungal species dropped significantly (Veerabahu et al. 2025). Michigan's invasive species program summarizes it as about half the expected diversity of native fungi, and reports golden oyster growing wild in Michigan's southern Lower Peninsula (Michigan Invasive Species Program).

Ohio State does not recommend it for outdoor cultivation in North America. The study's lead author asks sellers to note that it should be grown indoors and not composted. If you grow it:

  • Grow it indoors only. No logs, no garden beds, no outdoor fruiting.
  • Do not compost the spent block or dump it outside. Seal it in a bag and put it in the trash.
  • Harvest before the caps flatten. The SARE booklet notes that picking at that stage also limits spore release.

If you would rather skip that, blue and pink oysters give you the cool room and warm room options without it.

FAQ

Which oyster mushroom is easiest to grow?

Blue oyster for a cool or normal room, pink oyster for a warm one. Ohio State names pearl and blue as the easy starting point, and both blue and pink are tagged beginner in our profile library.

Is pink oyster faster than blue oyster?

Yes. Pink runs 20 days from spawn to the end of the first harvest in its profile, against 25 for blue. From a colonized kit, it is 10 days for pink and 13 for blue.

Can you put a pink oyster block in the fridge?

No. Pink oyster is tropical, its profile says never to cold shock it, and the SARE grower booklet says the pink strain it grew cannot survive temperatures below 40 °F (4 °C). Keep the block warm and eat the harvest within a couple of days.

Why are my blue oysters turning grey?

The room is too warm. Blue oyster holds its color best below about 18 °C (64 °F), and its profile fruits at 14 °C (57 °F). Some warm blue strains also turn steel grey as they mature, so pick them young.

Can you grow blue, pink and golden oyster at the same time?

Not well in one space. Their fruiting temperatures are 10 °C (18 °F) apart, 14 °C (57 °F) for blue and 24 °C (75 °F) for pink. Grow them one after another as the seasons change, blue in winter and pink in summer.

Is golden oyster safe to grow at home?

It is a common edible, but it is invasive in North American forests. Grow it indoors only and put the spent block in the trash, not the compost.

item.title: What is the dark magic mushroom?
item.description: A tiny Florida mushroom, Galerina indica, makes both psilocybin and deadly amatoxins. What the study found, and what it means for foragers.
item.content:encoded:
The dark magic mushroom is Galerina indica, a thumbnail-sized brown mushroom found on a rotting, moss-covered palm trunk in a Florida wetland. A University of Florida team reported in Current Biology on 2026-11-11 that it makes both psilocybin, the psychedelic compound in magic mushrooms, and amatoxins, the toxins that make death caps deadly. It is the first mushroom known to make both. Amatoxins damage the liver, symptoms can start 6 to 24 hours after eating and then seem to fade, and no wild mushroom should be eaten on a guess. If someone has eaten an unknown wild mushroom, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away, or 911 if they are very sick.

Short answer

Until this month, mushrooms fell into two camps. Some make psilocybin and some make amatoxins, and nobody had found one that makes both. Galerina indica does. Researchers at the University of Florida nicknamed it the "dark magic mushroom," and their paper came out in Current Biology on 2026-11-11.

This post is science and safety information. It covers what the researchers actually reported, why the combination matters to anyone who picks wild mushrooms, and what to do if someone eats the wrong one. It is not a guide to finding, growing or eating anything. Shroom Labs does not sell spores, cultures or psilocybin products.

What is the dark magic mushroom?

It is a small brown mushroom in the genus Galerina, the "little brown mushroom" group. The species is Galerina indica. The largest ones the team found stood about 0.2 inches (0.5 cm) tall, with caps about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide, so a cluster fits on a thumbnail.

Two things made it worth a second look. Some Galerina species were already known to make amatoxins. And this one turned blue when handled, which is a trait seen in some psilocybin mushrooms. The team tested for both compound families and found both.

The word "magic" is the news hook. The word "dark" is the point: the same mushroom carries a toxin that can destroy a liver.

Who found it, and where?

According to the University of Florida, Andrew Kunik found the mushroom while documenting fungi at the UF/IFAS Ordway Swisher Biological Station. Science News reports it was in 2025, on a decaying, moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik was a student researcher in the lab of Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist who is also Florida's state mycologist.

The paper's team came from the University of Florida, the University of Utah, Ohio State University and the University of California, Berkeley. The preprint lists five Galerina specimens collected in the southeastern United States. Three were Galerina indica. Two were other Galerina that the team could not match to a named species.

Science News notes that Galerina indica had not been reported in Florida before, and that earlier researchers had described how it looks and found DNA markers for it, but nobody had mapped its chemistry or its genes.

How did researchers know it has both compounds?

They used mass spectrometry, which measures the mass of the molecules in a tissue sample, and then they checked the genes. Here is what the open preprint says, in plain terms.

  • Chemistry. Tiny samples of dried mushroom tissue, 1 to 2 milligrams each, were analyzed by tandem mass spectrometry. The team ran authenticated standards for comparison, and ran two control mushrooms alongside: an Amanita known to make amatoxins but not psilocybin, and a polypore expected to make none of the compounds. The controls behaved as expected.
  • Result. All three Galerina indica collections contained psilocybin and psilocin plus two amatoxins. Of the other two Galerina, one had psilocybin and psilocin but no detectable amatoxins, and the other had neither.
  • Genes. A genome analysis found the gene sets that build both kinds of compound. Psilocybin comes from a compact five-gene cluster. Amatoxins come from a different gene system.
  • Open data. The raw mass spectra are public in the MassIVE repository under accession MSV000101888.

One caution about sources. The method details above come from the open bioRxiv preprint posted in July 2026, because I could not open the Current Biology page. The journal version is the version of record, so check it if a number matters to you.

Why is a mushroom with psilocybin and amatoxins so dangerous?

Because one effect hides the other. Psilocybin is the reason people go looking for magic mushrooms. Amatoxins are a delayed poison. A person who eats an unidentified little brown mushroom expecting a psychedelic effect could be taking in a liver toxin, and the first warning may come hours later.

The researchers' own words are blunt. Smith said these mushrooms are small and brown like hundreds of other species, and that they are hard to tell apart "even for a trained expert." Mycologist Anne Pringle, who was not part of the study, told Science News that when people ask "can I eat it?" about a new mushroom, "this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable."

I did not find any report of a human poisoning from Galerina indica in the sources I read. The point is not that people are being poisoned by this species. The point is that the lines people rely on, "magic mushrooms are one thing and poisonous mushrooms are another," do not hold.

How do amatoxins poison people?

Amatoxins are ring-shaped peptides. According to the preprint, they shut down an enzyme called RNA polymerase II, which cells need to make proteins. Liver cells take up amatoxins from the gut, and that is why the liver is hit hardest.

The CDC describes the pattern in three phases:

  1. Hours 6 and later. Delayed abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Liver tests can still look normal.
  2. Hours 12 to 36. Lab signs of liver injury, trouble with blood clotting and kidney injury.
  3. Days 2 to 6. Worsening liver function that can progress to liver and kidney failure. Some patients need a liver transplant.

The CDC adds that amatoxins are not destroyed by cooking or other food preparation, and that the delay can contribute to deaths. It puts the modern case fatality rate at 10 to 20 percent based on earlier case series. In a recent Northern California cluster of Amanita poisonings from foraged mushrooms, 39 cases were reported to poison control between November 2025 and March 2026. Of those, 3 patients needed liver transplants and 4 died. That cluster involved Amanita, not Galerina, but amatoxins are the same family of toxins.

The California Department of Public Health describes the same trap: early symptoms can go away within a day, and that brief improvement can be deceptive, because serious liver damage can still develop 48 to 96 hours after eating.

What is alpha-proamanitin, and is it less dangerous?

This is the most interesting chemistry in the paper. The main amatoxin in Galerina indica was one nobody had seen in a mushroom before. The team named it alpha-proamanitin. It is built like alpha-amanitin, the most common deadly amatoxin, except that it lacks a single hydroxyl group on a proline residue. Alpha-amanitin itself was not detected in any Galerina indica sample.

The authors reason that this missing group could make alpha-proamanitin a weaker blocker of RNA polymerase II, based on lab studies of related amatoxins. They also say amatoxins missing that group "remain toxic." And they float a hypothesis that picking up psilocybin genes may have taken pressure off the lineage to make the stronger toxin.

Please do not read "possibly less potent" as "safe." Nothing in the sources I read measures the toxicity of alpha-proamanitin in people. It is a structural argument and a hypothesis. The only safe reading is that this mushroom carries amatoxins.

Can you tell it apart from other mushrooms by looking?

No, and the researchers say so. Smith said it is "hard to differentiate from others, even for a trained expert." The team needed DNA sequencing of three genetic regions to place the species, plus mass spectrometry to confirm what was in it.

The blue bruising is a good example of why looks fail. In this case, a mushroom that stains blue turned out to carry a deadly toxin as well as psilocybin. Bruising color, size, habitat and cap shape are clues for a mycologist with a microscope. They are not a safety test for someone standing in a yard.

The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia poison center gives the same advice for every wild mushroom: the close similarities make it hard for anyone but a trained expert to tell them apart, so the best prevention is to assume that no wild mushrooms are safe to eat.

How did one mushroom end up with both?

Through horizontal gene transfer, which is when genes move between unrelated species instead of passing from parent to offspring. Live Science calls it widespread among fungi. The preprint says both the psilocybin and amatoxin pathways were already known to have moved between distantly related fungi.

The team's reading is that the Galerina indica lineage already made amatoxins, and later picked up the psilocybin gene cluster. The psilocybin genes sit in a different order than in other psilocybin mushrooms, which suggests the cluster was rearranged after it arrived. Smith estimated the transfer at about 15.5 million years ago. Kunik noted it may have happened in two separate events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, and that the family tree needs more specimens to settle it.

Why would a mushroom carry both? Nobody knows yet. One hypothesis is defense: an animal that eats mushrooms would have a hard time evolving resistance to two unrelated chemicals. Kunik called that a speculation, and the UF release says amatoxins may help protect mushrooms from animals that eat them but their exact role is not clear.

Does this change anything for people who pick wild mushrooms?

It breaks a tidy sorting rule. The University of Florida release opens by noting that mushrooms seemed to split into two camps, magic and poisonous. Galerina indica sits in both, and it is a small, brown, easy-to-miss species, exactly the kind a person could gather by mistake.

Federal law lists psilocybin and psilocin as Schedule I. For the legal picture on mushrooms and spores, see our dated state by state summary in Are mushroom spores legal in the United States?. Nothing here is advice to go looking for any mushroom.

For anyone who forages for food, the practical rules are old and still right:

  • Do not eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified that exact mushroom in person. Photos in an app are not enough.
  • Cooking, drying and freezing do not remove amatoxins.
  • Early stomach symptoms that clear up are not a sign you are fine.

What should you do after eating an unknown wild mushroom?

Act right away, before any symptoms.

  • In the United States, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 if the person is very sick.
  • Do not wait for symptoms. Amatoxin poisoning is dangerous because the first symptoms come late.
  • Keep a sample of what was eaten if you can, bagged and clearly marked as poison, so a mycologist can identify it. A photo of the mushroom and where it grew also helps.
  • Tell the hospital exactly what was eaten and when, even if the person feels better.

The North American Mycological Association says the same: if you suspect someone has eaten an amatoxin mushroom, do not wait for symptoms to appear.

Why do known species in a controlled chamber make more sense than foraging?

Because the biggest risk in this story is not knowing what you have. Foraging asks you to identify a mushroom from a few clues, and this paper shows that even experts needed a lab for it.

Shroom Labs builds a controller that is species agnostic. It holds temperature, humidity, fresh air and light for whatever species is running in the chamber. The idea that follows from this news is simple: if you want to grow mushrooms, buy a known, named culture from a reputable supplier, grow that known species in a chamber you control, and never treat a wild mushroom as food on a guess. A chamber does not make an unknown mushroom safe. A known species from a known source takes the identification problem off the table.

We write grow guides for culinary species such as oyster and lion's mane in Grow mushrooms at home, and the grow hub lists the rest. Psilocybin mushrooms are illegal to grow, possess or sell in most places, and what you do about your local law is up to you. We publish reference information on them for research and harm reduction only.

FAQ

Is the dark magic mushroom the same as a magic mushroom?

No. Magic mushrooms usually means species that make psilocybin, mostly in the genus Psilocybe. The dark magic mushroom is Galerina indica, a different genus. It makes psilocybin and also amatoxins, which are the toxins that make death caps deadly.

Is Galerina indica really the first mushroom with both compounds?

The researchers say so. Study first author Andrew Kunik told Live Science that no mushroom species in any group had been known to produce both at the same time. The preprint adds that no phylogenetically placed Galerina species had been reported to produce psilocybin before this study.

How deadly are amatoxins?

Amatoxin poisoning has a modern case fatality rate of 10 to 20 percent, according to the CDC. The North American Mycological Association puts it at about 10 percent in the United States and Canada with good medical care and about 50 percent without prompt treatment. Cooking does not remove the toxins.

Has anyone been poisoned by Galerina indica?

None of the sources I read describe a poisoning by this species. Its relatives in the Galerina marginata group, sometimes called funeral bells, are well documented as deadly.

Is alpha-proamanitin safer than alpha-amanitin?

Nobody knows. The authors argue from structure that it may be a weaker blocker of RNA polymerase II, but they also say amatoxins like it remain toxic, and no toxicity data for people are reported.

What should I do if I think someone ate a poisonous mushroom?

Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the United States right away, or 911 if they are very sick. Do not wait for symptoms, because amatoxin symptoms are delayed.

Where is the original study?

It is Kunik et al., "The dark magic mushroom co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin," Current Biology, 2026. The DOI is 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041. An open preprint is on bioRxiv and PubMed Central.

item.title: How to fruit a shiitake block
item.description: A shiitake block needs about 9 weeks of colonizing and browning before it fruits. Browning, soak and cold shock timing, and fruiting numbers, cited.
item.content:encoded:
Let the block colonize in the dark, rest it under low light until the outside turns brown and hard, then shock it cold and fruit it cool. Our shiitake profile colonizes for 42 days at 24 °C (75 °F), browns for 21 days at 21 °C (70 °F) under 12 hours a day of about 200 lux, then gets a 12 to 24 hour cold shock at 5 to 10 °C (41 to 50 °F). It fruits for 10 days at 16 °C (61 °F) and 85% humidity. Soak the block in cold water for up to 24 hours if it feels light. In a 2024 study, pins showed 2 to 3 days after a 24 hour cold soak and the mushrooms were full size 4 to 5 days after that.

What does a shiitake block need to fruit?

Time, a brown skin, and a cold, wet signal. Shiitake is not like oyster, where you cut a hole in a white bag and get mushrooms in a week. A white shiitake block is not ready. It has to sit under low light until the outside turns brown and tough, and then it needs a jolt of cold water or cold air before it pins.

These are the stages and numbers from our shiitake profile:

ColonizationBrowningCold shockFruiting
Days4221110
Temperature24 °C (75 °F)21 °C (70 °F)5 to 10 °C (41 to 50 °F), in a fridge16 °C (61 °F)
Humidity88%80%90%85%
LightDark12 h a day, about 200 lux, blueDark12 h a day, about 90 lux, blue
Chamber fan15 s every 60 min20 s every 45 min15 s every 60 min35 s every 12 min

That is 63 days of colonizing and browning before the shock, and 74 days from spawn to the end of the first flush. Plug your start date into the grow timeline calculator to get calendar dates for each stage.

If your block came from a kit already brown and firm, it is past the browning stage. Start at the soak.

Why does a shiitake block have to turn brown first?

The brown coat is the block's bark. A 2024 study from Korea's National Institute of Forest Science describes what it does: once browning is complete, the block resists contamination even in open air and loses less moisture, which helps the mushrooms develop. If browning is incomplete, the block is treated as contaminated and a good crop is not expected (Kim et al. 2024).

The brown film is triggered by light. A 2019 genetics study calls light induced browning of the mycelium an important step for shiitake yield and quality (Yoo et al. 2019). That is why our profile keeps colonization dark and turns the light on for the browning rest.

You do not need much light for it. Kim et al. cite earlier work that found high browning efficiency at 200 lux, whatever the light source, with blue LED browning best. A 2018 study using LED light to brown sawdust blocks at 20 °C for 60 days got the best browning at a low 1.5 µmol/m²/s of red and blue light. Its strongest settings, 20.5 µmol/m²/s LED and 300 lux fluorescent, browned less (Koo et al. 2018). So our profile uses 12 hours a day at about 200 lux and stops there. More light is not better for browning.

How long should a shiitake block brown?

Longer than you want to wait. Our profile gives the block 42 days dark and 21 days under light, 63 days in all, and the profile note says to wait for full white and then browning and not to fruit early. Treat 63 days as the minimum and go by the block, not the calendar.

The research backs patience. In a Penn State study, sawdust blocks given a 116 day spawn run produced two to three times the yield (biological efficiency) of blocks given 58 days, and the mushrooms were generally larger (Royse 1985). Kim et al. put the usual browning culture for sawdust shiitake at 100 to 150 days. In their own trial, blocks got 60 days dark and then 40 or 60 days of light, and 40 days under blue light beat white light on yield in both strains tested (Kim et al. 2024).

How do you know a shiitake block is ready to fruit?

A 2024 study tracked shiitake blocks through five stages before it fruited them (El Sebaaly et al. 2024):

  1. Mycelium run: the substrate is fully covered by a thin layer of white.
  2. Coat formation: the white sheet hardens over the whole surface.
  3. Bumps: clumps of mycelium form a popcorn texture.
  4. Browning: the outside turns dark brown and dry.
  5. Coat hardening: the brown coat hardens.

They waited for the end of stage 5 before shocking. Popcorn bumps alone mean the block is getting close, not that it is ready. When most of the block is brown and the skin feels firm and leathery, it is time.

Step by step: fruiting a shiitake block

  1. Colonize in the dark. Keep the bag closed at around 24 °C (75 °F) until it is fully white. Our profile allows 42 days.
  2. Brown it under low light. Leave the bag closed, drop to around 21 °C (70 °F), and give it 12 hours a day of low light, about 200 lux. Our profile runs this rest at 80% humidity, a bit drier than colonization, for 21 days or longer.
  3. Check for a firm brown skin. Wait until the bumps have browned and the coat has hardened. White patches mean it needs more time.
  4. Take it out of the bag. Cut or peel the plastic off. Two of the block studies below say they opened or peeled the bag before the cold soak.
  5. Soak or chill it. If the block feels light, submerge it in cold water with a weight on top for up to 24 hours. If it still feels heavy and wet, a night in the fridge at 5 to 10 °C (41 to 50 °F) for 12 to 24 hours does the same job. The next two sections cover timing.
  6. Fruit it cool and damp. Move it to around 16 °C (61 °F) and 85% humidity with 12 hours of low light and steady fresh air. Mist the air, not the caps.
  7. Watch for pins in 2 to 3 days. In the 2024 study, pins showed 2 to 3 days after the soak and mushrooms reached full size 4 to 5 days after that.
  8. Harvest at 50 to 75% open. Pick while the gill edges are still rolled under. Twist from the base or cut flush with the block.
  9. Rest it, then repeat. Give the block about 2 weeks to recover, then soak again for the next flush.

How long should you soak a shiitake block?

Up to 24 hours in cold water is what the block studies used. Here is what each one did:

StudySoakWhat happened
Sawdust blocks (Sabota et al. 2004)24 h in tap water, weighted down, six soakings over the seasonPlain water was the control. Adding sugar to the soak lowered yield
Lebanese University, 1 kg bags (El Sebaaly et al. 2024)24 h in ice, bag removedPins in 2 to 3 days, full size 4 to 5 days later
Bag logs (Annepu et al. 2019)15 min in ice cold water, 4 to 6 °C (39 to 43 °F), bag peeledSame cold soak repeated for the second and third flush

The soak does two jobs: it wets the block and it chills it. A 15 minute ice cold dip is mostly a cold signal. A 24 hour soak also gives the block time to take up water.

Ohio State Extension gives the rule growers use for shiitake logs: the closer the log temperature is to the water temperature, the longer the soak. Their example is 6 to 24 hours in summer and 2 to 3 days in spring or fall (Ohio State Extension 2022). That is for logs. Every block study above stayed at 24 hours or less, so use that as your ceiling for a block. Do not add sugar to the soak water. In the 2004 trial, sucrose in the soak cut mushroom numbers and yield in both strains.

Does shiitake need a cold shock?

It needs a change, and cold is the most reliable one. Ohio State says temperature and moisture changes trigger shiitake to fruit (Ohio State Extension 2022). NCAT's ATTRA guide, a USDA funded grower program, says a dropping temperature triggers it, and that growers soak logs to start fruiting (NCAT ATTRA 2026).

Our profile's cold shock is 12 to 24 hours at 5 to 10 °C (41 to 50 °F), a range the profile notes credit to Stamets. A fruiting chamber cannot get that cold, so if you run the profile on a Shroom Labs chamber, this one stage happens in your fridge. Put the block in, then apply the fruiting stage when it comes back out. A cold water soak from the tap or with ice in it gives the same signal if your fridge is full.

Strain matters here. NCAT says warm weather strains fruit best with highs around 70 to 80 °F (21 to 27 °C), cool weather strains at roughly 50 to 65 °F (10 to 18 °C), and wide range strains respond well to forced fruiting. Check the temperature notes from whoever sold you the block. Our profile is a warm weather block strain.

What temperature, humidity, light and fresh air does shiitake need to fruit?

Cool, damp, lit, and well aired. Our profile fruits at 16 °C (61 °F) with warnings below 12 °C (54 °F) and above 21 °C (70 °F). The published numbers line up:

  • Temperature. NCAT gives 60 to 70 °F (15 to 21 °C) for shiitake fruiting. Ohio State gives 55 to 65 °F (13 to 18 °C) for pinning. The 2024 block study fruited at 16 °C (61 °F), and Kim et al. at 18 °C (64 °F).
  • Humidity. Our profile holds 85%. Ohio State asks for at least 85% while pinning, and NCAT gives 85 to 95% for fruiting in general. The block studies ranged from 80% (Kim et al.) to above 90% (El Sebaaly et al.).
  • Light. Light is required for normal shiitake fruiting, and only pigmented pins went on to expand in the classic lab work (Leatham and Stahmann 1987). Ohio State says enough light to read a newspaper at arm's length is enough. Our profile runs 12 hours a day at about 90 lux as a labeled default, because no shiitake specific fruiting lux was found for the chamber. The 2024 block study used 2,000 lux, so brighter room light is fine. Do mushrooms need light? has the numbers for other species.
  • Fresh air. Our profile jumps from a 20 second fan run every 45 minutes while browning to 35 seconds every 12 minutes while fruiting. Kim et al. held carbon dioxide at 1,000 ppm in their fruiting room. A block on an open shelf gets enough. A block in a closed tote does not.

Our two other shiitake profiles push the cap on purpose. The donko profile pins for 6 days at 13 °C (55 °F) and 95%, then fruits for 14 days at 15 °C (59 °F) and 75% for a thick, rounded cap. The flower cap profile fruits at 14 °C (57 °F) and only 60% so the dry air splits the cap skin into a white pattern. Neither is the place to start. Cracked caps on a regular grow mean the air is too dry, not that you have made flower shiitake. See dry, cracked mushroom caps.

When do you harvest shiitake?

When the cap is 50 to 75% open and the gill edges are still rolled under. Ohio State says picking at 100% open shortens shelf life, delays the next flush and invites pests. Twist the mushroom off by the stem, or cut it flush with a sharp knife, and touch only the stem because bruised caps and gills discolor fast (Ohio State Extension 2022).

Cool them to 33 to 35 °F (about 1 to 2 °C) as fast as you can, in a basket or paper bag, not a plastic bag. Ohio State notes frost free fridges tend to dry mushrooms out.

How do you get a second flush from a shiitake block?

Rest it, then soak it again. After the first harvest, the 2024 block study kept its blocks in the dark at 22 °C (72 °F) and 60% humidity for two weeks, then soaked them in ice for another 24 hours (El Sebaaly et al. 2024). NCAT gives 7 to 14 days of rest between flushes in general and notes later flushes give diminishing returns. The 2004 trial soaked its blocks six times in one season (Sabota et al. 2004).

The rest matters because the block just spent its stored energy and a lot of water. Soaking it again the day after harvest skips the recovery. Expect the second flush to be smaller. In the 2024 study, every substrate gave fewer mushrooms on the second harvest than the first.

Why is my shiitake block not fruiting?

Most stalled shiitake blocks are one of these:

  • It is not brown yet. A white or patchy block was shocked too early. Put it back under 12 hours of low light and wait.
  • It never got a signal. A block kept warm with no soak and no cold spell can sit for weeks. Soak or chill it.
  • The room is too warm for the strain. A cool weather strain in a 75 °F (24 °C) room will sit. Check the strain notes.
  • It dried out. A light, hard block needs a long soak.
  • It is in the dark or sealed in a tote with no air.
  • It was soaked again right after a harvest with no rest.

Mushroom grow kit not growing walks through each of these causes in order.

FAQ

How long does it take a shiitake block to fruit?

About 9 weeks before the first shock on our profile, 42 days to colonize and 21 days to brown. Kim et al. put the usual browning culture for sawdust shiitake at 100 to 150 days. After the shock, expect pins in 2 to 3 days and mushrooms 4 to 5 days later.

How long do you soak a shiitake block?

Up to 24 hours in cold water, weighted under. Two of the block studies soaked for 24 hours, and a third did a 15 minute dip in water at 4 to 6 °C (39 to 43 °F).

Can I put a shiitake block in the fridge to shock it?

Yes. Our profile uses 12 to 24 hours at 5 to 10 °C (41 to 50 °F), which is what a fridge does. Bring it straight out to cool, damp, lit fruiting conditions afterward.

Does a shiitake block need light?

Yes, twice. Low light, about 200 lux for 12 hours a day, browns the skin, and light is needed again for normal fruiting.

Why are my shiitake caps cracking?

Dry air. Raise the humidity toward 85% and mist the air, not the caps. Our flower cap profile does this on purpose at 60% humidity.

Sources

  • Koo et al. 2018, Browning technology for shiitake in sawdust using LED source, Journal of Mushrooms 16(4)
